newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - UK sheepdog case highlights need for RSPCA.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - UK sheepdog case highlights need for RSPCA.

text.p: Britons are famous for being a nation of soppy animal lovers who worry more about the welfare of their pets than they do about fellow humans.
Yet after almost 175 years, there is still a need for the country's most famous animal charity, the RSPCA (Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals).
Just last week, a farmer who triumphed in televised sheepdog trials was convicted of cruelty to five of his collies.
Three of Gwyn Jones's dogs were in such a poor state they had to be destroyed and two others are being looked after in RSPCA kennels.
The court was told that all the dogs were emaciated and dirty, had skin problems and were kept in unhygenic conditions. Heart-breaking pictures appeared in national newspapers.
Jones was fined 2,000 pounds ($3,270) and ordered to pay the RSPCA's costs of 1,750 pounds. But he was not banned from keeping dogs.
This is something the RSPCA is battling to change.
BANNING IS KEY

"I think it denies logical justification that one in four of the people we prosecute who could be disqualified, aren't," Richard Davies, chief officer of the inspectorate, told Reuters in an interview before the Jones case.
"We certainly believe that anyone who has been accused and convicted of cruelty to animals should automatically be disqualified."
Jones was not disqualified because without dogs, he could not run his hill farm in the Welsh region of Snowdonia.
The RSPCA say this is not a valid reason for allowing a cruel owner to keep animals.
"Just because someone needs a car for work doesn't prevent them from being disqualified for drink-driving," Davies said.

Davies stressed that he wasn't complaining about the courts, but said a common sentencing policy -- where all those convicted of cruelty are automatically banned -- was the only way to keep a lid on burgeoning cruelty statistics.

"We're not interested in fines or prison sentences. We want banning orders. That's the most effective way of keeping the cruelty rates down -- making sure that someone who's already offended isn't given the opportunity to re-offend," he said.
CRUELTY ON THE RISE
Dogs and cats remain the predominant victims, according to national RSPCA cruelty statistics published last month.
Convictions of cruelty to dogs were up 16 percent in 1996 to 892 while a rising cat population saw offences against cats rise by 27 percent to 235, a trend the RSPCA is keen to nip in the bud.

"People genuinely believe that having a cat gives them fewer responsibilities as a pet owner. That's simply not true," Davies said. "They are making a terrible mistake if they believe that cats require less attention, less love, less finance than a dog."
Davies said that economic hardship was a catalyst to pet neglect.
"If you're struggling, vet bills can make a difference. Chances are people won't cut back on other areas.
"It doesn't matter what animal you're having, you really have to think it out very carefully. It's going to be costly and it's going to be demanding of your time."
WHAT HAPPENS TO RESCUED ANIMALS?
RSPCA inspectors try to persuade cruel or neglectful owners to sign over an animal to their care so it can be found a new home.
If the owner refuses, the animal stays at an RSPCA-run establishment until its case is heard and the court decrees that it can go to another home.
Once in RSPCA care, the animal can start a "socialisation" procedure, and while some abused pets can take months to recover physically and mentally, others are grateful for a second chance.
"With just a little bit of care over a relatively short period of time you can change a cruelty victim into a superb family pet. Animals are incredibly forgiving," Davies said.
The Millbrook Animal Centre in Chobham in southern England is one such place which looks after and re-homes animals.
The crucial factor is human interaction, according to Millbrook's manager Tony Glue.

"If they were left in kennels all day, they'd go stir-crazy," he said, pointing to a row of around 20 dogs. Employers and volunteers walk the dogs, while a behavioural analyst deals with animals with emotional problems.
FINDING THE RIGHT HOME
The RSPCA is determined to prevent a recurrence of cruelty. That's why every potential owner is thoroughly vetted before being allowed to adopt an RSPCA animal.
"Some people say its very difficult to get an animal from the RSPCA, but we owe it to that animal to find it a good home," said Inspector Karen Renton.
Potential owners are asked to complete a form where they describe their living circumstances, give the number and age of children in the house, and state whether they have any other pets.
They are also asked to give permission for home visits. If they refuse, then they've got something to hide, according to the RSPCA.
And anyone who thinks getting a rescue animal is a cheap option should think again.

The cost of adopting an RSPCA rescue dog, which includes micro-chipping and neutering, ranges from 60 pounds to 103 pounds, while a cat could set you back as much as 53 pounds. ($ = 0.610 British Pounds)
